sets.g: Passage A represents a formal and polite submission for a tenancy agreement. The language is also precise, and it contains details of the event. Passage B represents a less formal submission for a tenancy agreement. It seems like a personal message to the recipient and is somewhat playful. As such, the response is perhaps familiar and friendly in return.
sets.p:
A. I appreciate the thoroughness of your submission. After careful review of all your documents, I am pleased to offer you a tenancy agreement. This will be an Assured Shorthold Tenancy, with a 6-month break clause. Please sign your name at the bottom of the page where indicated to confirm the offer.
B. I have looked through your documents over the weekend. Although your employment reference was thin, I would like to accept you as my new tenant. Feel free to give me a call over the next few days to sort out details and to sign the contract.
i: This is great news, thanks for accepting me. I aim to move in, in the next few weeks or so if that is alright?
B
The language is more casual than formal. Especially the last phrase – asking a question in an off-hand manner. This is more appropriate in response to passage B.
Cool – I am a little busy tomorrow and the day after, but I will contact you sometime after that.
B
The language is very perfunctory. Starting a sentence with ‘Cool’ suggests that the submitter and receiver know each other.
It is with the greatest of pleasure that I hear this news. Thank you for taking the time to look through my submission.
A
The language is polite and formal. This is a more appropriate response to passage A upon hearing of their success in the submission. The phrases are elongated and are idiomatic of politeness.
The contract sounds reasonable and I will sign it without question.
B
The response is abrupt and to the point. While it would work for passage A, it is more appropriate to passage B given the present casual tone.
I am pleased with this result. However, I must question the 6-month break clause as that seems disadvantageous for my position.
A
Not only is the language is polite and formal, but it also recognises the 6-month clause which is only present in passage A. Therefore, this is a response for passage A.

sets.p: It is good that you are happy about the tenancy (gift / offer / offering). I notice your concern with the 6-month (claus / clause / claws), but I am afraid I must insist on this. While I appreciate the (precarious / precariously / precariousness) situation that this could potentially place you in, I openly admit that I will only use this if (exhaustively / fully / intimately) necessary from my position. I do not wish to see my beloved property mistreated in any way. I have no doubt in your clean-living standards, but relinquishing this power makes me (appear / be / feel) most uncomfortable.
i: “It is good that you are happy about the tenancy (gift / offer / offering).”
Gift
Offer
Offering
B
Given the context, to form a tenancy contract is neither an offering nor a gift. It is however an offer, a proposal. As such, ‘offer’ is the correct answer.
“I notice your concern with the 6-month (claus / clause / claws)…”
Claus
Clause
Claws
B
This is a spelling choice. ‘Claus’ is a name, whilst ‘Claws’ are part of as such neither make sense here. ‘Clause’ is the correct spelling, indicating a provision in the contact.
“While I appreciate the (precarious / precariously / precariousness) situation…”
Precarious
Precariously
Precariousness
A
This is a conjugation challenge. Given that the adjective is describing ‘situation’, precariously and precariousness do not make sense. ‘Precarious’ is the only choice that makes grammatical sense.
“I openly admit that I will only use this if (exhaustively / fully / intimately) necessary from my position
Exhaustively
Fully
Intimately
B

Although, ‘exhaustively’ would work as it is an adverb, it is awkward and not suited to the context. ‘Intimately’ is, once again, an adjective, but is confusing and somewhat bizarre in the given context. ‘Fully’ necessary is clear and is part of an English phrase in common use. Therefore, ‘fully’ is the correct answer.
“…relinquishing this power makes me (appear / be / feel) most uncomfortable.”
Appear
Be
Feel
C

Appearing uncomfortable does not seem appropriate given the context for that is not the focus of the situation. ‘Be’ most uncomfortable does not make sense. ‘Feel’ most uncomfortable is appropriate and suggests that the previous clause is resulting in unease. Therefore, this is the correct answer.

sets.p: I understand your wish to kept the 6-month tenancy clause. I am willing to except this if I am able to bring pets into the property. I currently have a few fish, that I keep in a tank, and do not want to apart with them. I am also an avid smoker, and it would be important to me that I am able to smoke out of the window thoroughout the day. I appreciate that these terms may not be appealing to you, but I believe them to be reasonable. Please let me know what you thought.
i: “I understand your wish to kept the 6-month tenancy clause.”
Keep
The past tense of ‘keep’ is in the passage which needs to be replaced with the present tense conjugation = keep.
“I am willing to except this…”
Accept

A classic problem of two words in English sounding the same but having very different meanings and spellings. ‘Except’ is odd and confusing given the context. With the ‘if clause’ needing confirmation, here we need to ‘accept’ the situation.
“…I keep in a tank, and do not want to apart with them.”
Part
‘Apart’ with them does not make grammatical sense. Given the situation of not wanting to lose fish, we do not want to ‘part’ with them. Therefore, ‘apart’ needs to be changed to ‘part’.
“I am able to smoke out of the window thoroughout the day.”
Throughout
This is a spelling problem. ‘Thoroughout’ out is not a word and needs to be replaced with ‘throughout’. The ‘o’ needs deleting.
“Please let me know what you thought.”
Think
The past tense of ‘think is in the passage which needs to be replaced with the present tense conjugation = think.

sets.p:
1. I do not like the sound of this agreement. I suggest you back out now and save yourself the trouble later.
2. That agreement sounds horrible. I do not know what you did but you have clearly done the wrong thing here.
3. Sounds good – I say go for it!
4. You have struck the deal of a lifetime. What are you waiting for?
5. I am not sure about this, I am afraid. There are some good parts, but there are also some serious cons.
i: I do not like the sound of this agreement. I suggest you back out now and save yourself the trouble later.
4th
This is a very negative response to the tenant. But it offers some advice so it is not all bad. Therefore, it is below neutral but above full negativity. As such it is ranked D.
That agreement sounds horrible. I do not know what you did but you have clearly done the wrong thing here.
5th
This response is very negative and even suggests the fault on the tenant. As such it is ranked E.
Sounds good – I say go for it!
2nd
This is a short, positive and uplifting response. Though given the other responses is not the most positive. As such it is ranked B.
You have struck the deal of a lifetime. What are you waiting for?
1st
This is an enthusiastically positive response with none more so. As such, this is ranked A.
I am not sure about this, I am afraid. There are some good parts, but there are also some serious cons.
3rd
This response is sceptical and explicitly states that there are pros and cons – right in the centre. As such, this is ranked C.

sets.p: I will be moving out of 28 Victoria Lane in two weeks’ time, and move into my new place at 159 Bluebird Avenue on the 27th of April. I am leaving all my furniture which you can add on to the inventory for the next tenant. I have asked some friends to help me with the move as I need to carry my fish tank down three flights of stairs to the ground floor. I have ordered a professional cleaner to service the room, so there should not be any deductions from my deposit. Thank you for the kind reference, I appreciate it.
i: This message was sent on the 13th of April.
True

True – Line 1 states that in two weeks from the message they will move into their new place. This future date will be 27th. Therefore, we must minus two weeks from this date to get the message sent date. 27 – 14 = the 13th of April. Therefore, this is true.
The tenant is leaving everything in their room for the next occupant.
False
False – Line 3 states that the tenant is taking their fish tank with them from the room.
On the 28th of April, the tenant will be living at 28 Victoria Lane.
False
False – Line 1 states that they are living 28 Victoria Lane and moving into 159 Bluebird Avenue by the 27th. Therefore, they will be living at 159 Bluebird Avenue on the 28th of April.
The property at 28 Victoria Lane is located on the third floor.
True
True – Line 3 states that they are going to have to descend three flights of stairs to the ground floor. Therefore, the property is located on the third floor.
The tenant is bringing five friends to help them with the moving.
Cannot Say
Cannot Say – There is no mention of this information in the passage. Therefore, we cannot say.

sets.g: Passage A represents a formal and considered message. The language is formal and professional. The response to this message must equally be formal and kindly, though perhaps distant and deferential. Passage B represents a less formal message. Equally positive, it is more familiar and casual. It is likely that the sender and the submitter know each other at least a little bit. As such, the response is perhaps slightly bold, familiar in return.
sets.p:
A. My apologies for the presumptuousness of my message, but I am enquiring as to the results of my medical examination. It has been nigh on three weeks now, and yet, I have heard nothing back from you, save an automated response.
B. Sorry for contacting you like this, but I am wondering if something happened to my medical results. I have not heard anything from you for a while now; it’s a little disconcerting.
i: I am sorry that you have had to wait this long. There are a few problems going on at the clinic. I cannot discuss them. The results will come your way shortly.
B

Though the opening apology is very formal, the remaining response is surprisingly revealing. The short, curt, phrase ‘I cannot discuss them’ suggests familiarity. The message better suits passage B in response.
Thank you for your follow up message. I greatly appreciate your concern regarding your medical results. Please do not worry, there has been a slight delay, but the results are on their way.
A
This language is polite, formal and reserved. ‘Greatly appreciate’ is a particular highlight of formal language. There is reassurance and professionalism. Therefore, this response suits passage A.
Thank you for contacting us once again. It is worrying that you have not been contacted further. We shall investigate how this occurred. Please accept my sincerest apologies.
A
This language is polite, formal and reserved. ‘Sincerest apologies’ is a particular highlight of formal language. There is reassurance and professionalism. Therefore, this response suits passage A.
It upsets me that you feel this way. Please hold on a little longer if you can – the results will be on their way soon.
A
Surprisingly vulnerable and intimate. However, the language style is professional and reassuring. As such, this response better suits passage A than passage B.
We are sorry about this. Someone will be contacting you in the next few days to discuss this issue.
B

While this response could potentially work for both passages, the response is not entirely warm and as such, not effectively professional. It would work better for a less serious situation as suggested by passage B.

sets.p: You contacted us earlier this month asking for the latest information (an / in / on) your medical examination. The results have come in and I am afraid I (had / has / have) some rather unfortunate news. While the results have ruled out (approximately / couple / some) of the more serious possibilities regarding your (condition / location / scenario), there are a few elements from your examination report that concerns us. Unfortunately, this means that we require you to (came / come / coming) back to the clinic for further testing.
i: “You contacted us earlier this month asking for the latest information (an / in / on) your medical examination.”
An
In
On
C
‘An’ and ‘in’ does not make sense given the context of the sentence. The only option is ‘on’, resulting in ‘on your medical examination’ which is the right use of language and correct answer.
“…I am afraid I (had / has / have) some rather unfortunate news.”
Had
Has
Have
C

This is a tense challenge. I ‘had’ some… refers to something that happened. Given the remaining passage, this does not work. I ‘has’ is not correct grammar. I ‘have’ some… presents the present tense in the passage which is the correct use of language.
“While the results have ruled out (approximately / couple / some) of the more serious possibilities…”
Approximately
Couple
Some
C

‘Couple’ requires a proposition which is non-existent in this context. ‘Approximately’ followed by ‘of’ does not make grammatical sense. ‘Some’ of, on the other hand, makes sense and is the correct answer.
“… more serious possibilities regarding your (condition / location / scenario), there are a few elements…”
Condition
Location
Scenario
A

This choice is based on the context as each technically work. ‘Location’ seems inappropriate as it bears little relation to medical examination results. ‘Scenario’ could be used abstractly to suggest the patients’ situation, however ‘condition’ directly address the concerns and discussion point of the patient.
“…this means that we require you to (came / come / coming) back to the clinic.”
Came
Come
Coming
B

Given the context of the phrase, it seems necessary that we require the present tense conjugation of the verb ‘to come’. As such, ‘came’, past tense, and ‘coming’, present continuous are inappropriate. The correct answer is ‘come’ which is available.

sets.p: Following my recent massage, thank you for the promptness of your response. It is no doubt worring to hear that I am not yet in the clear. I will of course come into the clinic for farther examination. I work full-time, Monday to Friday, so will find coming into the clinic difficult during these times. I am available Saturday or Sunday morning if that works for you? I gather these are not ideal times, but there was not much I could do aside leave work for a day – which I cannot afford.
i: “Following my recent massage…”
Message
This is a spelling problem. ‘Massage’ which is bizarre in this context needs to be edited to be ‘message’ which indicates the necessity of the response.
“It is no doubt worring to hear…”
Worrying
This is a spelling problem. ‘Worring’ is not a word, it is missing the ‘y’. The correct spelling should be ‘worrying’.
“…come into the clinic for farther examination.”
Further

‘Farther’ examination does not make sense. Farther is a comparative adverb for something that is far. What we require is a word which indicates ‘continued’. The correct answer is ‘further’ which makes sense given the context.
“…there was not much I could do…”
Is
This is a tense challenge. ‘Was’ is the past tense of ‘to be’. However, given the context of the passage, we require the present tense. The present tense of ‘to be’ = ‘is’.
“…leave work for a day – which I cannot afford.”
Leaving
This is a tense challenge. ‘Leave’ is the present tense of ‘to leave’. However, given the context of the passage, we require the present continuous. The present continuous of ‘to leave’ = ‘leaving’.

sets.p:
1. I’m not optimistic about the results. But go in for treatment sooner rather than later.
2. You have nothing to worry about, I am here to support you if need be!
3. I wouldn’t even bother trying at this point if I were you.
4. I know you may be nervous, but I believe you will get through this.
5. I realise the treatment is not ideal, but it shall all be fine.
i: I’m not optimistic about the results. But go in for treatment sooner rather than later.
4th

The response is negative, though it is sympathetic. The last phrase offers some advice. There is little warmth in the language. It is not the most negative statement here but cannot be ranked as positive or ambivalent. As such, it is ranked D.
You have nothing to worry about, I am here to support you if need be!
1st
Given that most of the responses are not overtly positive, this is the most supportive. Not only does it reassure, but it offers implicit and practical support. As such, this is ranked A.
I wouldn’t even bother trying at this point if I were you.
5th
This response is very negative and offers nothing but despair. As such, it is ranked E.
I know you may be nervous, but I believe you will get through this.
2nd
This response is kindly and reassuring. Though it does not offer practical support like response 2, it gives hope by believing the outcome will be positive. As such, this is ranked B.
I realise the treatment is not ideal, but it shall all be fine.
3rd
This is reassuring but not overtly so. It is surprisingly neutral in tone, suggesting that it is just ‘fine’. As such, this is ranked C.

sets.p: Our clinic is five minutes’ walk away from Baker Street station. We can be found opposite the Mandarin estate building. Our opening hours are 09:00 – 18:30, Monday to Friday and 10:00 – 13:00 on Saturday. You can book appointments online. When you come in for a booking, make sure you have proof of identity on you as well as access to your National Insurance number. If you require urgent medical attention on the Sunday, or over the Christmas period, please ensure you call the GP emergency help line.
i: The clinic is ten minutes’ walk from Regents’ Park station.
Cannot Say
Cannot Say – There is no mention of Regents’ Park station in the passage. As such, we cannot say for definite. Remember to go on only the information provided to you within the passage.
There is an appointment next week at 13:30 on Saturday.
False
False – Line 3 states that the clinic’s opening hours are from 10:00-13:00 on Saturday. As such, an appointment cannot be held at 13:30 on Saturday.
Appointments to the clinic can be booked using the Internet.
True
True – Line 4 states “you can book appointments online”. As such, this is true.
The GP emergency help line will allow an appointment at 11:30.
Cannot Say
Cannot Say – There is no mention of appointment times for the GP emergency help line.
To attend an appointment at the clinic, one only needs their National Insurance number.
False
False – Line 5 states that one requires not only their National Insurance number, but also their “proof of identity”. As such, this statement is false.

sets.g: Passage A represents a formal and considered message. The language is serious and professional. The response to this message must equally be formal and kindly, though perhaps distant and deferential. Passage B represents a less formal message. Though serious, it is more familiar and less strict in its use of language. It is likely that the sender and the applicant know each other at least a little bit. As such, the response is perhaps slightly bold, familiar in return.
sets.p:
A. Welcome to Overseas Hotels. Thank you for booking with us today. Check-in is from 10:30 am onwards. We wish you a wonderful time during your stay.
B. Thanks for booking with our hotel! We look forward to meeting you – someone will be there to greet you at the reception desk.
i: I very much look forward to my trip. Factoring in for delays, I should arrive on time for check-in.
B
“I very much look forward to my trip” seems to be directed to a person rather than an establishment. There is a casualness of tone that feels more appropriate to passage B.
Great – I am excited to be staying at the hotel!
B
The language is very informal and almost certainly expressed in a non-serious way. As such, this response is for passage B.
Thanks for the info, I shall see you then.
B
The language is quite flippant and unconcerned about professionalism. It is brief and to the point. Since it is not particularly deferential, it is better suited as a response for passage B.
Thank you for the message, I shall do my best to arrive in time for check-in.
A

The language is gracious and deferential. Not only the ‘thank you’ but the soft acknowledgement of character ownership present in the second part of the phrase – “I shall do my best”. This is better suited as a response for passage A.
I am pleased. I believe I made the right choice in booking my stay with you.
A
The language is formal, reserved and very polite. The emotional distant in the statement indicates that this response is better suited to passage A.

sets.p: My journey to your hotel has not been as (basic / loose / simple) as I would have hoped. Upon arrival to the airport, I noticed that my handbag was missing. I contacted the airport (authorities / bureaucracy / power) but was unable to communicate with them as I (could / wood / would) not speak their language. Three hours passed before my bag was found, only (after / before / during) which could I leave the airport and make my way to the hotel. I apologies for missing the check-in time, but I (hope / hoped / hoping) you appreciate my misfortune in the matter.
i: “My journey to your hotel has not been as (basic / loose / simple) as I would have hoped.”
Basic
Loose
Simple
C

‘Loose’ is a strange word to describe the journey. ‘Basic’ can work, though it feels awkward in contrast to the other option ‘simple’ which more appropriate describes a journey. Given the context, ‘simple’ is more synonymous with ‘straightforward’ which seems more appropriate here. As such, simple is the correct answer.
“I contacted the airport (authorities / bureaucracy / power) but …”
Authorities
Bureaucracy
Power
A

‘Power’ does not make sense here for there is no description of what kind of power that is. ‘Bureaucracy’ again is not appropriate here as it is ill-defined. ‘Authorities’ is appropriate and best articulates that the individual was trying to speak to those in charge of the airport.
“…unable to communicate with them as I (could / wood / would) not speak their language.”
Could
Wood
Would
A

‘Wood’ is nonsensical in this context and seems more likely to be a misspelling of ‘would’ – which, it seems strange in this scenario. The individual could not communicate with the authorities because they would not speak their language feels unlikely or bizarre. ‘Could’ not speak their language feels realist and is more appropriate. As such, ‘could’ is the correct answer.
“…my bag was found, only (after / before / during) which could I leave the airport...”
After
Before
During
A

Given the context of the passage, leaving the airport during a situation finding a bag seems bizarre. Leaving ‘before’ finding the bag seems even more so. Leaving the airport ‘after’ finding the bag seems most sensible and is the correct answer.
“I apologies for missing the check-in time, but I (hope / hoped / hoping) you appreciate my misfortune in the matter.”
Hope
Hoped
Hoping
A

This is a tense challenge. ‘Hoped’ is the past tense of ‘to hope’ which is grammatical incorrect in the phrase which is in the present. ‘Hoping’ is the present continuous of ‘to hope’ can only work with a ‘to be’ antecedent, either ‘am’ or ‘was’ which there is not. As such, this cannot work. ‘Hope’ is the present of ‘to hope’ which works in this phrase and is the correct answer.

sets.p: The first part of my voyage took me up the mountains. I could not believe how impression the mechanisms were for scaling the incline. At the top, I arrived at the heighest temple. I sought to be placid and deferential. Following that latest journey, I frequently the local eateries and savoured the cuisine. It was delightfully, I can assure you, though it all take a little getting used to.
i: “I could not believe how impression the mechanisms were …”
Impressive
‘Impression’ in the middle of the sentence makes no sense. Truthfully, it is a spelling challenge - the correct answer being ‘impressive’ which suggests that the mechanisms were effective.
“At the top I arrived at the heighest temple.”
Highest
‘Heighest’ is not a real word and as such this is a spelling challenge. The correct spelling is ‘highest’ which is the answer here.
“I frequently the local eateries and savoured the cuisine.
Frequented

‘Frequently’ does not make sense in this phrase. What we need is a word that describes going to the ‘local eateries’. As such, the nearest word to this is ‘frequented’ which is given as a clue by the incorrect in its place.
“It was delightfully, I can assure you…”.
Delightful

The phrase ‘it was delightfully’ does not make grammatical sense – the main culprit being ‘delightfully’ which is not given a word for it to describe. However, what needs to be is to put focus on the being rather than the describer. As such, the correct answer is to change the conjugation to ‘delightful’.
“…I can assure you, though it all take a little getting used to.”
Took

This is a tense challenge ‘Take’ is the present tense of ‘to take’ which in this phrase does not work from it required the past tense. The past tense of ‘to take’ is ‘took’, which therefore is the correct answer.

sets.p:
1. Wow. I am not at all impressed with these photos. Just awful.
2. I am amazed at how uninspiring you made the trip seem with those photos.
3. I am jealous – looks like you had a lovely time!
4. Pretty cool, do you recommend going?
5. Seemed like a fun trip though these photos are not great.
i: Wow. I am not at all impressed with these photos. Just awful.
5th
This response is quite callous in its intent and language. The final words ‘just awful’ epitomises this exchange. This is clearly a very negative response and as such is ranked E.
I am amazed at how uninspiring you made the trip seem with those photos.
4th
This response is snarky in language and mean-spirited with intent. There is an element of sarcasm too. It is negative, however given response 1, it is not the most. As such, this is ranked D.
I am jealous – looks like you had a lovely time!
1st
The language is infatuating and kindly. The ‘lovely time!’ phrase in particular highlights this. Given the context of the other phrases, it is the most positive. As such, it is ranked A.
Pretty cool, do you recommend going?
2nd

The language is very casual but positive and fairly uplifting. It seems to be a correspondence between friends of a kind. This is not as positive as response 3 which is more overt in its positivity. As such, this is ranked B.
Seemed like a fun trip though these photos are not great.
3rd
This is somewhat double-edged compliment which is nice and not at the same time. As such, it best sits in the middle of the ranking as being both positive and negative.

sets.p: The mountain is a famous tourist destination. It is popular for climbers to scale to the summit. From the base, it typically takes 7-9 hours to climb to the top, and 4-5 hours to descend. While it is possible to climb the mountain in a single day, it is not recommended. ‘Bullet Climbers’, as they are called, can easily succumb to altitude sickness – the only remedy is to come down the mountain immediately. One does not need to be an experienced climber to attempt the mountain challenge, but a reasonable level of fitness is required to avoid undesirable problems.
i: An experienced climber could scale to the mountain summit and back in 11 hours.
True
True – Lines 2 and 3 outline the potential times for climbing. Taking the quickest times given, 7 and 4 respectively, it is possible to be done in 11 hours.
Anyone is allowed to climb the mountain.
False
False – Line 5 states that one must have a “reasonable level of fitness” before climbing.
‘Bullet Climbers’ will suffer from altitude sickness.
Cannot Say
Cannot Say – Though it is perhaps likely, given what is stated in line 5, there is no mention of it happening always. We do not have enough information and as such cannot say.
An inexperienced climber could take 15 hours to scale to the mountain summit and back.
True

True – Taking the maximum times from the recommendations of line 2 and 3, which are 9 and 5 respectively, we get 14 hours. However, one could take longer if they require. There is not a restriction to their time. The times given are merely typical or suggested. As such, this is a true statement given the information in the passage.
Climbers suffering from altitude sickness should take a break where they are.
False

False – According to line 5, climbers suffering from altitude sickness should descend the mountain immediately as this is the only remedy. Therefore, this statement is false given the information in the passage.
